title: Count the Longest Rising Subsequences
statement:
You get an integer array nums. A rising subsequence keeps some of the values in their original order, and each kept value is strictly larger than the one before it.

Let L be the length of the longest rising subsequence. Return how many rising subsequences have length L. Subsequences are told apart by the positions they use, so two picks with the same values at different positions count twice.

examples.why: The longest length is 3, reached by 1, 4, 5 and 1, 2, 5 and 1, 2, 3.
Equal values cannot follow each other, so the longest length is 1, and each of the three positions is its own subsequence.
Length 3: pick 2 or 1, then 4 or 3, then 6 or 5. The choices multiply: 2 · 2 · 2.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: First solve the easier question: for each index i, how long is the longest rising subsequence that ends at i?

Next to that length, also keep how many subsequences reach it at i. When an earlier j with nums[j] < nums[i] gives a longer length, it replaces the count; when it gives the same length, its count adds on.
The answer adds up the counts of every index whose length equals the overall longest length, not just the last index.

explain.intuition:
The classic longest-rising DP stores len[i], the best length of a rising subsequence that ends at i. To count, store a second number alongside: cnt[i], how many subsequences of length len[i] end at i. Every such subsequence is some best subsequence ending at an earlier j with a smaller value, plus nums[i].

So for each smaller earlier value j: if len[j] + 1 beats len[i], it is the new best and cnt[i] becomes cnt[j]; if it ties, cnt[i] += cnt[j]. Finally, sum cnt over all indices that reach the overall maximum length, because longest subsequences can end in many places. A Fenwick tree over value ranks can merge those (length, count) pairs in O(log n) per index for the O(n log n) version.
steps: For each i and every j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: if len[j] + 1 > len[i], set len[i] = len[j] + 1 and cnt[i] = cnt[j]; if equal, add cnt[j] to cnt[i].
Return the sum of cnt[i] over all i with len[i] = L.
pitfalls: Adding 1 to the count on a tie instead of adding cnt[j]. The third example then returns far fewer than 8.
Returning cnt of the last index or of the first index that reaches the longest length. Longest subsequences can end at several indices.
Allowing equal values to chain. The rule is strictly rising, so [3, 3, 3] has length 1.

solutions.title: Check every subset
solutions.idea: Try every set of positions, keep the rising ones, and count those with the greatest length.

solutions.title: Length and count per ending index
solutions.idea: Alongside the best length ending at i, keep how many subsequences reach it. Longer replaces the count; equal adds to it.

solutions.title: Fenwick tree over value ranks
solutions.idea: Index a Fenwick tree by the rank of each value. A prefix query over smaller ranks returns the best (length, count) pair to extend; then store the new pair at this value's rank.

followups: Return one of the longest subsequences, not just how many there are.
